query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of cerium into the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy will promote the in situ formation of stable, cerium‐rich oxide surface domains that simultaneously enhance low-temperature oxidation activity, improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and inhibit catalyst sintering during long-term operation—all without increasing platinum-group-metal usage.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst with minimal platinum-group metals.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with a low concentration (e.g., around 5 atomic percent) of cerium (or equivalently incorporating a dispersed ceria phase) during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exhaust gas compositions representative of transient and low-temperature (≤150 °C) operation containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO, with accelerated aging protocols simulating lifetime mileage degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of cerium‐rich oxide clusters or thin surface layers that segregate during catalyst processing/aging.
generation.mechanism: The Ce‐rich domains are expected to boost oxygen mobility and redox cycling at the catalyst surface, lowering reaction energy barriers for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation while also acting as barriers that adsorb or block poisoning species (H2O and NO). Additionally, these domains can hinder the sintering or agglomeration of active metal particles, thereby enhancing lifetime durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified catalyst, the cerium‐doped variant should show appreciably higher catalytic activity at low temperatures, better resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO, and less performance degradation over extended aging cycles.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (oxidation rates, poisoning resistance, and durability) of the unmodified near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst under identical exhaust and aging conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for transient low-temperature (<150 °C) operations and under exhaust compositions that include typical automotive poisons; benefits are contingent on maintaining low platinum-group-metal content and may be specific to the concentration range of cerium doping.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal cerium concentration, its precise interaction with the other alloy constituents, and the magnitude of improvement in poisoning resistance and durability over extended real-world conditions remain to be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two catalyst samples: one from the base near‐equiatomic alloy and the other doped with approximately 5 at.% cerium. Subject both to catalytic oxidation tests using simulated exhaust conditions (including CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO) at temperatures at or below 150 °C. Apply an accelerated aging protocol to mimic vehicle lifetime exposure. Compare catalytic performance, resistance to poisoning (via adsorption studies), and structural stability (via in situ TEM/XPS analysis) over time.
measurements: Low-temperature oxidation conversion rates of CO and hydrocarbons
Extent of poisoning effects (e.g., drop in activity in the presence of H2O and NO)
Structural characterization of surface oxides and particle size distribution pre- and post-aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-doped catalyst does not show a statistically significant improvement in catalytic activity, poisoning resistance, and durability relative to the unmodified catalyst—or if adverse phenomena (e.g., unwanted phase segregation, increased sintering, or detrimental interactions with exhaust components) are observed—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
